newsitem.title: GERMANY: Three EU states boost broadcasts to ex-Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: Three EU states boost broadcasts to ex-Yugoslavia.

text.p: The short-wave radio broadcasters of Germany, Britain and France want to boost reception of their programmes in former Yugoslavia to ensure people have access to free media, Germany's Deutsche Welle said on Monday.

Dieter Weirich, the station's director, said in a statement that foreign broadcasting was a "voice of freedom, which is more important than ever" and that he hoped to get European Union money to secure more effective frequencies.

He told Reuters: "Most states in former Yugoslavia don't have full press freedom. If democratic developments are going to happen you need to have this. The biggest problem is the endangering of press freedom."
Weirich said foreign media had a special meaning in former Yugoslavia. "In communist times the BBC and Deutsche Welle had a special meaning, people trusted them. It's still the case."
Deutsche Welle, Britain's BBC and Radio France International already cooperate on their broadcasts to the Balkans.
The EU grant they are hoping for would let them rent medium-wave frequencies from Albania to give better reception, particularly for their Serbian, Croatian and Bosnian language reports.
Weirich said the move was a way of promoting media freedom throughout former Yugoslavia, and that without a free press there would be no political stability in the region.
"I'm very optimistic. We hope to get an answer at the end of January or the beginning of February. If we get the financial support we can begin in early spring 1997," Weirich said.
Earlier this month Deutsche Welle supported an independent Serbian radio station, B-92, after the station was shut down by the authorities.
It transmitted original B-92 reports on events in Belgrade and other Serbian towns during its daily Serbian news programme.
Tens of thousands of people have been marching daily through the frozen streets of Belgrade for a month to protest against the authorities' annulment of local election results.
The state media have remained silent on the demonstrations or concentrated on attacking the opposition.
Deutsche Welle carries three Serbian language programmes a day but its special transmissions of B-92 reports have now ended as the independent broadcaster is back on air.
